what_it_does: Rowhammer is a hardware attack where repeatedly reading the same row of DRAM memory causes electrical interference that can randomly flip bits in adjacent rows — potentially corrupting data an attacker does not own. In cloud environments, many customers' virtual machines share the same physical server, managed by a piece of software called a hypervisor (which acts like a landlord enforcing isolation between tenants). Prior Rowhammer attacks have let one tenant corrupt another tenant's memory, but corrupting the hypervisor itself — which would give an attacker control over the entire server — was thought to be blocked by the hypervisor's own defenses. HyperHammer demonstrates a new attack path that circumvents KVM's (a widely used open-source hypervisor) protections and successfully flips bits in hypervisor-owned memory from within a guest virtual machine, effectively escaping the isolation boundary and compromising the host. The abstract does not specify the precise technique used to locate and hammer hypervisor memory, so the exact mechanism is uncertain.
